questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A publisher in China finds that the state's orders for printed textbooks keep growing; explain why textbooks were being printed in such large numbers, and say what happened to the volume of print from the sixteenth century onwards.

markingPoints.description: States that the imperial state in China was, for a very long time, the major producer of printed material

States that China possessed a huge bureaucratic system recruiting personnel through civil service examinations, and that textbooks for these were printed in vast numbers under the sponsorship of the imperial state
States that from the sixteenth century the number of examination candidates went up, and that this increased the volume of print

From the sixteenth century the number of examination candidates went up, and that increased the volume of print.

questions.stem: A student traces printing in China from hand printing to mechanical presses; show in steps (a) how books were printed by hand and why the traditional Chinese ‘accordion book’ was folded and stitched at the side, (b) what new technology arrived, from where and when, (c) which city became the hub of the new print culture and whom it catered to, and (d) what change followed for printing.

markingPoints.description: States that books were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks
States that because both sides of the thin, porous sheet could not be printed, the traditional Chinese ‘accordion book’ was folded and stitched at the side
States that Western printing techniques and mechanical presses were imported in the late nineteenth century as Western powers established their outposts in China
States that Shanghai became the hub of the new print culture, catering to the Western-style schools

answerScheme.modelAnswer:

(c) Shanghai became the hub of the new print culture, catering to the Western-style schools.
(d) From hand printing there was a gradual shift to mechanical printing.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A publisher in Edo wants thousands of identical ukiyo prints made from one design; show in steps (a) what the art form ukiyo means and who was born in Edo in 1753, (b) in what order a commissioned theme became a printed image, and (c) what happened to the artist’s original drawing.

markingPoints.description: States that ukiyo means ‘pictures of the floating world’, depicting ordinary human experiences, especially urban ones
States that Kitagawa Utamaro, born in Edo in 1753, was widely known for his contributions to this art form
States that publishers like Tsutaya Juzaburo identified subjects and commissioned artists who drew the theme in outline
States that a skilled woodblock carver pasted the drawing on a woodblock and carved a printing block
States that the original drawing was destroyed and only prints survived

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) Ukiyo means ‘pictures of the floating world’, the depiction of ordinary human experiences, especially urban ones, and Kitagawa Utamaro, born in Edo in 1753, was widely known for his contributions to it.
(b) Publishers like Tsutaya Juzaburo identified subjects and commissioned artists who drew the theme in outline; then a skilled woodblock carver pasted the drawing on a woodblock and carved a printing block.
(c) In the process, the original drawing was destroyed and only prints survived.

questions.stem: A student reads a diary entry written in 1791 by a London publisher about what his customers were buying; show in steps (a) who wrote the entry and what he recorded about the sale of books, (b) how the poorer country people spent their winter evenings before that period and what they did with the same evenings afterwards, and (c) name the two books the entry says these readers were sent out to buy.

markingPoints.description: States that the writer was the London publisher James Lackington, in 1791
States that the sale of books in general had increased prodigiously within the last twenty years, and that the poorer sort of farmers and even the poor country people in general were reading
States that before that period they spent their winter evenings relating stories of witches, ghosts and hobgoblins
States that now they shorten the winter night by hearing their sons and daughters read them tales, romances and so on
Names the two books as Peregrine Pickle’s Adventure and The History of Joseph Andrews

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) In 1791 a London publisher, James Lackington, wrote in his diary that the sale of books in general had increased prodigiously within the last twenty years, and that the poorer sort of farmers and even the poor country people in general were among those reading.
(b) Before that period they spent their winter evenings relating stories of witches, ghosts and hobgoblins; now they shorten the winter night by hearing their sons and daughters read them tales, romances and so on.
(c) John, going to town with a load of hay, is charged not to forget to bring home Peregrine Pickle’s Adventure, and Dolly, sent to sell her eggs, is commissioned to purchase The History of Joseph Andrews.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
By the seventeenth century, as urban culture bloomed in China, the uses of print diversified and print was no longer used just by scholar-officials. Merchants used print in their everyday life, as they collected trade information, and reading increasingly became a leisure activity. The new readership preferred fictional narratives, poetry, autobiographies, anthologies of literary masterpieces and romantic plays. Rich women began to read, and many women began publishing their poetry and plays; wives of scholar-officials published their works and courtesans wrote about their lives.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one or two lines. (i) Name two uses that print was put to in seventeenth-century China by people other than scholar-officials. (ii) Which kinds of writing did the new readership prefer? (iii) A student says only men wrote books in this period; use the case to show why that is not correct.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Merchants collected trade information, and reading became a leisure activity. (ii) Fictional narratives, poetry, autobiographies, anthologies of literary masterpieces and romantic plays. (iii) Rich women read and many published their poetry and plays, wives of scholar-officials published their works, and courtesans wrote about their lives.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
Kitagawa Utamaro, born in Edo in 1753, was widely known for his contributions to an art form called ukiyo, ‘pictures of the floating world’, or the depiction of ordinary human experiences, especially urban ones. His prints travelled to contemporary US and Europe and influenced artists like Manet, Monet and Van Gogh. Publishers like Tsutaya Juzaburo identified subjects and commissioned artists who drew the theme in outline. Then a skilled woodblock carver pasted the drawing on a woodblock and carved a printing block to reproduce the painter’s lines. In the process, the original drawing was destroyed and only prints would survive.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one or two lines. (i) In what order did a commissioned theme become a printed image in Edo? (ii) What happened to the artist’s original drawing? (iii) How can you tell from the case that these prints were made for readers beyond Japan?

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) A publisher such as Tsutaya Juzaburo identified the subject, an artist drew it in outline, and a skilled woodblock carver pasted the drawing on a woodblock and carved a printing block. (ii) It was destroyed; only prints survived. (iii) The prints travelled to contemporary US and Europe and influenced artists like Manet, Monet and Van Gogh.
